chapters.title: Chapter 1: Why Sectors Matter More Than You Think

lessons.title: How Sectors Are Classified: NSE Indices, AMFI, and Screener.in Industry Tags

body.text: A sector label is someone else's judgment call, not a law of nature. Before you pick peers, read a fund factsheet, or check your sector exposure, know who assigned the label, at what level of detail, and where it stops describing how the business actually earns money.

children.text: The last lesson established that you must compare companies within the same sector. That raises an obvious question: who decides which sector a company belongs to? In India, three sources shape almost everything you will see as an investor: the classification used by the stock exchanges, the industry list AMFI uses for mutual fund portfolio disclosures, and the tags on data platforms like Screener.in. They are closely aligned today, but they are not perfect, and knowing their limits will save you from bad comparisons.
The Four-Level Classification Used by NSE and BSE

Indian exchanges use a hierarchical, four-level structure. Every listed company sits in exactly one bucket at each level, moving from very broad to very specific. Think of it as a postal address: country, state, city, street.

stats.label: Macro-Economic Sectors
stats.context: Broadest level, e.g. Financial Services, Commodities

stats.label: Basic Industries
stats.context: Most granular, e.g. Private Sector Bank

body.caption: The Same Four Companies, Classified Level by Level

children.text: Notice what happens with HDFC Bank and Bajaj Finance. At the top two levels they look identical. Only at the Industry level do they split, into Banks and Finance. That split matters enormously: a bank funds itself with cheap current and savings account deposits, while an NBFC like Bajaj Finance cannot take those deposits and relies more on borrowing from banks and bond markets. Their cost of funds, regulation, and risk profile are different. The level you compare at decides whether your comparison is sharp or sloppy.

body.title: Pick the Right Level
body.question: You want to judge whether Kotak Mahindra Bank's cost of funds is competitive. Which classification level gives you the most useful peer group?
body.explanation: Cost of funds depends heavily on deposit franchise and ownership. Public sector banks and private banks differ in branch networks, deposit mix, and government ownership, so the sharpest comparison is against other private sector banks such as HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, and Axis Bank. The broader levels would mix in insurers, NBFCs, and brokers, which have entirely different funding models.

children.text: NSE Sectoral Indices: The Labels You See Every Day

When a business channel says 'banks dragged the market today', it usually means the Nifty Bank index fell. NSE Indices builds sectoral indices such as Nifty Bank, Nifty IT, Nifty FMCG, Nifty Pharma, Nifty Auto, Nifty Metal, Nifty Realty, and Nifty PSU Bank from companies in the relevant classification buckets. Two things to keep in mind. First, these indices are weighted by free-float market capitalisation, so the largest companies dominate: a big move in HDFC Bank or ICICI Bank alone can swing Nifty Bank. Second, they only include large, liquid stocks, so the index is not a picture of the whole industry. Nifty Bank tells you very little about small finance banks.

columns.label: Sectoral (e.g. Nifty IT, Nifty Pharma)
points: Built from one sector or industry
Constituents share the same business model and drivers
Moves strongly together because the same forces hit every company

columns.label: Thematic (e.g. Nifty India Consumption, Nifty Infrastructure)
points: Built around an idea that cuts across several sectors
A consumption index can hold FMCG, auto, telecom, and retail stocks together
More diversified than a sectoral index, but still a concentrated bet on one story

children.text: AMFI and Mutual Fund Sector Disclosures

If you invest through mutual funds, the sector labels you see in a factsheet or monthly portfolio disclosure come from the industry classification that AMFI publishes for the industry. This is why an HDFC Mutual Fund factsheet and an SBI Mutual Fund factsheet label the same stock the same way, which makes sector exposure comparable across fund houses. AMFI is also the body that publishes the twice-yearly list sorting stocks into large cap, mid cap, and small cap. Do not confuse the two: market cap tells you how big a company is, sector tells you what it does.

body.label: SEBI rule for sectoral and thematic funds
body.value: Minimum 80% of assets in the stated sector or theme
body.context: Set under SEBI's 2017 mutual fund scheme categorisation. The remaining 20% can go into other equities, debt, or cash.

body.title: Illustrative Portfolio: A Banking and Financial Services Fund
Is This Fund Within the Rule?
body.prompt: Look at the illustrative banking and financial services fund above. Add up the percentage of the portfolio held in financial services stocks: private sector banks, public sector banks, NBFCs, and insurance. What is the total, in percent?
body.explanation: 48 + 12 + 14 + 9 = 83%. That clears SEBI's 80% minimum. Notice that 60% of the fund sits in banks alone, so even inside a 'financial services' fund, one industry drives most of the returns. Always look one level below the fund's name.

children.text: Screener.in: Where You Will Actually Use This

On a Screener.in company page, the peer comparison section shows the company's classification path, from broad sector down to the specific industry. Each level is clickable and opens a list of every listed company in that bucket, with sortable columns for market cap, P/E, ROCE, and more. This is the fastest way to build a peer set. The habit to build: always click down to the most specific level that still gives you at least four or five meaningful peers, then remove any company whose business mix clearly does not match.

markDefs.definition: A company that runs several unrelated businesses under one listed entity, each with its own economics, for example refining, telecom, and retail.

children.text: Every company gets one label, even when it runs several very different businesses. This is where most classification errors come from, and the biggest culprit is the
. The label is typically assigned based on where the largest share of revenue comes from, which may not be where the profits or the future growth come from.

body.caption: Common Classification Traps in Indian Markets

cells: Jio in telecom and Reliance Retail are large, fast-growing businesses with completely different drivers from refining
Cigarettes contribute the large majority of segment profit, and it also runs paperboard, packaging, and agri businesses
It is largely a holding company; its value comes from stakes in Bajaj Finance and the insurance businesses
Also owns large listed IT services subsidiaries (LTIMindtree and L&T Technology Services), which behave like IT stocks

body.title: Is Reliance a Fair Peer for IOC?
body.scenario: You are analysing Indian Oil Corporation. On Screener.in, you open the oil and gas peer group and see Reliance Industries sitting at the top by market cap. Reliance trades at a noticeably higher P/E than IOC, BPCL, and HPCL. A friend concludes that the state-owned oil marketing companies must be deeply undervalued compared to Reliance.
body.prompt: Is Reliance a fair peer for judging IOC's valuation? What would you do instead?
body.modelAnswer: Not a clean one. IOC, BPCL, and HPCL are primarily refiners and fuel marketers whose earnings swing with crude prices, refining margins, and government influence on fuel pricing. Reliance has a refining and petrochemicals business, but a large part of its value comes from Jio and Reliance Retail, which the market values more like telecom and consumer businesses. Its higher P/E partly reflects those businesses, not a mispricing of IOC. Compare IOC against BPCL and HPCL, which share its business model and ownership structure. If you want to compare with Reliance at all, look only at its oil-to-chemicals segment results, which are disclosed separately in segment reporting.

body.text: Segment reporting is your fix for conglomerates. Listed companies with multiple businesses disclose revenue and profit for each reportable segment in their quarterly results and annual report. When the label and the segment mix disagree, trust the segment mix.

body.title: Fill in the Blank
body.textWithBlank: When a company runs several different businesses, check its ___ reporting in the quarterly results to see where revenue and profit actually come from.
body.explanation: Segment reporting breaks results down by business line. It tells you whether the sector label reflects where the money is really made.

body.title: Build a Clean Peer Set for Any Stock
steps: Open the company page on Screener.in and note its classification path from broad sector to basic industry
Click down to the most specific level that still gives you at least four or five listed peers
Open the latest quarterly results or annual report and check segment reporting for how revenue and profit split
Remove any peer whose main business differs meaningfully, even if it shares the label
Split peers further if ownership or model differs, for example private vs public sector banks, or banks vs NBFCs
Note which NSE sectoral or thematic index the company belongs to, so you know which index moves it tracks

body.label: Screener.in
body.description: Search any listed company, then use the classification links in the peer comparison section to see every company in the same sector or industry.

points: Indian exchanges classify every listed company in four levels: macro-economic sector, sector, industry, and basic industry
The level you compare at matters; HDFC Bank and Bajaj Finance share a sector but split into Banks and Finance at the industry level
NSE sectoral indices are free-float market cap weighted, so a few large stocks dominate them and small companies are left out
Mutual fund sector disclosures follow AMFI's industry classification, and SEBI requires sectoral and thematic funds to hold at least 80% in their stated sector or theme
Screener.in's classification links are the fastest way to build a peer set, but always check the peers' actual business mix
Conglomerates like Reliance, ITC, and L&T carry one label but run businesses with very different drivers; use segment reporting to see the real mix

body.text: Classification categories, counts, and individual company labels are revised periodically by the exchanges and AMFI. Always check the current classification on NSE, BSE, AMFI, or Screener.in. Company examples are for educational illustration only and are not investment recommendations.
